questions.question: Process execution consists of a cycle of:
questions.explanation: Process execution alternates between CPU execution (CPU burst) and waiting for I/O (I/O burst).

questions.question: A histogram of CPU-burst times typically shows:
options: A large number of long bursts
A large number of short bursts
An equal distribution of all burst lengths
questions.correctAnswer: A large number of short bursts
questions.explanation: CPU-burst distributions characteristically show a large number of short CPU bursts and a small number of long CPU bursts.

questions.question: The CPU scheduler makes decisions when a process does all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Switches from running to waiting state
Switches from running to ready state
questions.explanation: CPU scheduling decisions occur when a process switches from running to waiting, running to ready, waiting to ready, or terminates—not during normal arithmetic instruction execution.

questions.question: Which scheduling scheme allows a process to keep the CPU until it terminates or switches to the waiting state?
questions.explanation: Under Nonpreemptive (cooperative) scheduling, once the CPU is allocated to a process, the process keeps the CPU until it releases it by terminating or switching to the waiting state.

questions.question: Preemptive scheduling can result in what problem when data are shared among several processes?
questions.explanation: Preempting a process while it is updating shared data can lead to Race conditions if another process accesses the inconsistent data.

questions.question: The module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler is the:
questions.explanation: The Dispatcher gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler by switching context, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper program location.

questions.question: The time it takes for the dispatcher to stop one process and start another running is called:
questions.explanation: Dispatch latency is the time required for the dispatcher to stop one process and start another running.

questions.question: The amount of time a process has been waiting in the ready queue is called:
questions.explanation: Waiting time is the sum of the periods a process spends waiting in the ready queue.

questions.question: A scheduling algorithm aims to minimize which of the following?
questions.explanation: Scheduling algorithms aim to maximize CPU utilization and throughput while minimizing turnaround time, waiting time, and response time.

questions.question: The phenomenon where short processes wait behind a long process in FCFS scheduling is called:
questions.explanation: In FCFS scheduling, short processes waiting for one long CPU-bound process to release the CPU is known as the Convoy effect.

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes?
questions.explanation: Shortest-Job-First (SJF) is provably optimal because moving a short process before a long one reduces the waiting time of the short process more than it increases the waiting time of the long process.

questions.question: How do operating systems typically implement SJF scheduling?
options: By predicting the next CPU burst using exponential averaging
By running all processes for 1 second first
By looking at the process file size
questions.correctAnswer: By predicting the next CPU burst using exponential averaging
questions.explanation: Because the exact length of the next CPU burst cannot be known in advance, the OS estimates it using exponential averaging of previous measured CPU bursts.

questions.question: The preemptive version of Shortest-Job-First (SJF) scheduling is:
questions.explanation: Shortest-Remaining-Time-First (SRTF) is the preemptive version of SJF, preempting the running process if a newly arrived process has a shorter burst than the remaining time.

questions.question: In Round Robin (RR) scheduling, what happens when a process's time quantum elapses?
options: The process is preempted and added to the end of the ready queue
The process receives a higher priority
questions.correctAnswer: The process is preempted and added to the end of the ready queue
questions.explanation: In Round Robin scheduling, when a process's time quantum expires, a timer interrupt preempts the process and places it at the tail of the ready queue.

questions.question: If the time quantum in Round Robin is extremely large, the scheduling algorithm behaves like:
questions.explanation: If the time quantum is very large, each process finishes its entire CPU burst before the quantum expires, causing Round Robin to degenerate into FCFS.

questions.question: In Round Robin, the time quantum should ideally be large with respect to the:
questions.explanation: The time quantum must be large compared to the context switch time so that context switching overhead remains a small fraction of CPU time.

questions.question: In priority scheduling, the CPU is allocated to the process with the highest priority. A common problem with this is:
questions.explanation: Priority scheduling can cause Starvation (indefinite blocking), where low-priority processes wait indefinitely because higher-priority processes keep arriving.

questions.question: What is the standard solution to the problem of starvation in priority scheduling?
questions.explanation: Aging prevents starvation by gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait in the system for a long time.

questions.question: A scheduling system where the ready queue consists of multiple queues with different algorithms is called:
questions.explanation: A Multilevel Queue scheduler partitions the ready queue into several separate queues, each with its own scheduling algorithm.

questions.question: A Multilevel Feedback Queue scheduler allows a process to:
options: Change its actual CPU burst length
questions.explanation: Unlike a fixed multilevel queue, a Multilevel Feedback Queue allows a process to move between queues based on its CPU burst behavior and waiting time.

questions.question: Which scheduling model resolves scheduling competition *within* the process (between user-level threads)?
questions.explanation: Under Process-contention scope (PCS), the thread library schedules user-level threads onto available LWPs, so competition for the CPU takes place among threads belonging to the same process.

questions.question: Kernel thread scheduled onto available CPU cores represents:
questions.explanation: To decide which kernel-level thread to schedule onto a physical CPU core, the kernel uses System-contention scope (SCS), where all threads in the system compete.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an architecture for Multiple-Processor Scheduling?
questions.explanation: Multiple-processor scheduling architectures discussed in the lecture include multicore CPUs, multithreaded cores, NUMA systems, and heterogeneous multiprocessing—not single-core pipelining.

questions.question: A smaller integer in priority scheduling typically represents:
questions.explanation: In the textbook and lecture convention, priorities are represented by integers where a smaller integer indicates a higher priority.

questions.question: The SJF algorithm is a special case of which scheduling algorithm?
questions.explanation: SJF is a special case of general Priority scheduling where the priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst length.

questions.question: Virtually all modern operating systems use nonpreemptive scheduling algorithms.
questions.explanation: Virtually all modern operating systems (including Windows, macOS, Linux, and UNIX) use preemptive scheduling algorithms.

questions.question: Throughput refers to the number of processes that complete their execution per time unit.
questions.explanation: Throughput is the measure of work done, defined as the number of processes completed per unit of time.

questions.question: SJF scheduling can be implemented exactly because the OS knows the precise length of all future CPU bursts.
questions.explanation: There is no way to know the exact length of the next CPU burst in short-term CPU scheduling; SJF must approximate it by predicting the next burst.

questions.question: In Round Robin scheduling, no process waits more than `(n-1)*q` time units if there are `n` processes in the ready queue and the time quantum is `q`.
questions.explanation: With n processes in the ready queue and time quantum q, each process gets 1/n of the CPU time in chunks of at most q time units, waiting at most (n-1)*q time units until its next turn.

questions.question: Aging can be implemented using a multilevel feedback queue.
questions.explanation: A multilevel feedback queue can implement aging by upgrading a process that waits too long in a lower-priority queue to a higher-priority queue.
